newsitem.title: CANADA: One tenth of Canadian troops battle Red River.
newsitem.headline: One tenth of Canadian troops battle Red River.

text.p: Canada mobilized a tenth of its soldiers to combat Manitoba's swelling Red River in the hope of saving lives at risk from rising water and high winds.

"If you took our commitments to Bosnia, Haiti and the Golan Heights, put them all together and multiplied by three, we still have more here," Major Douglas Martin said outside a military's briefing theater where topographic maps highlighted southern Manitoba's most vulnerable communities.
Some 6,700 of Canada's 65,000 soldiers drew battle lines against the worst Manitoba flood since 1852.

The Red crested at the Canadian border town of Emerson on Monday as soldiers manned a massive mud dike under assault from 60 kilometer per hour winds pushing waves that held back a 29 kilometer wide lake.
Three hundred sailors, including 50 divers, navigated what has become known as the "Red Sea" as it sprawled over an area more than twice the size of New York City.
"You think of people and equipment that are only used on the coast and it gives you an idea of how big this lake is," Martin said.

More than a quarter of sandbagged dikes around farmsteads buckled under the relentless crashing of white capping waves, Manitoba Emergency Management Organization executive coordinator Harold Clayton said after a helicopter tour.
Three dozen inflatable navy speed boats fanned out across the lake to evacuate or rescue any people at risk and handle underwater repairs, Lieutenant Chris Henderson said.
The last time this many sailors were deployed in-land was during Manitoba's 1950 flood when 100,000 Winnipeggers were forced from their homes when the Red River flooded, he said.
But 220 army engineers and infantry troops along with 200 earth moving machines worked to extend a stone, sand and earth dike to defend the low lying southwestern flank of Winnipeg.
"We've been going around the clock since Thursday with the army. It'll hold," Manitoba Highway projects engineer Lester Dean said as he hauled sandbags along the diked highway.

Manitoba Premier Gary Filmon descended in a helicopter which whipped up the drizzling rain already falling on the First Combat Engineer Regiment as it feverishly shored up the dike while flood waters creeped toward them only miles away.
"Under normal conditions, we believe this dike will hold," Filmon said.
On the other side of the dike infantry troops dug into mounds of sand to fill bags in a last ditch effort to protect homes in case the dike does not hold.

"The people here are grateful to see such a huge response. I've never been involved in something this large," Sgt. Paul Alexander said as he filled bags to protect a retirement home of 20 people in Sanford, just north of the dike.
Still, emergency officials placed more than 2,000 people on evacuation standby in case the dike breaches.
"People here are in a state of denial. This is really bad," Capt. Craig Landry said in Sanford.
